source.title: The History of Herodotus, Volume 1
source.attribution: Herodotus, The History of Herodotus, Volume 1 (trans. G. C. Macaulay), Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: History began as a way to keep great deeds and their causes from being forgotten
cards.body:
Herodotus was born around 484 BC in Halicarnassus, today's Bodrum on the Turkish coast. He travelled widely, asked questions everywhere, and around 430 BC published what he called his "Inquiry". The Greek word for it, historia, gave us the word history.

His opening line states two aims: that great deeds by Greeks and non-Greeks alike should not be forgotten, and that the causes of their wars should be remembered. He wanted to know why things happened, not just what happened.

That is still the best reason to study the past. A list of dates teaches little; asking what caused a conflict, and how it might have gone differently, teaches a lot.
cards.quote: and especially that the causes may be remembered for which these waged war with one another
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶1
cards.apply_it: Pick one conflict in the news this week and write down three causes you think led to it.

quiz.question: Besides recording great deeds, what did Herodotus most want readers to remember?
quiz.explanation: His opening sentence says he wrote especially so that the causes of the wars would be remembered.

cards.title: When two sides tell a story differently, say so before you pick a winner
cards.body:
Herodotus opens with the old tales of why Greeks and Persians became enemies. Persian storytellers blamed Phoenician sailors for kidnapping Io, a princess of Argos in Greece. The Phoenicians told it differently: they said Io left with them of her own free will.

Rather than pretend to know, Herodotus sets the two versions side by side and declines to rule on legends no one could check. He then moves to events he could actually investigate.

It is a good habit for any disagreement, from a family quarrel to a news story. Hear each side's version, notice where they clash, and be honest about which parts nobody can prove.
cards.quote: concerning these things I am not going to say that they happened thus or thus
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶6
cards.apply_it: Next time you hear about a dispute, ask yourself: what would the other side say happened?

quiz.question: How did Herodotus handle the clashing Persian and Phoenician stories about Io?
options: He set them side by side and refused to rule on them
quiz.explanation: He reported both accounts and said he would not claim either was what really happened.

cards.title: A king who couldn't keep his pride private lost his throne
cards.body:
Herodotus tells a legend about Candaules, king of Lydia in what is now western Turkey, around the 680s BC. Candaules was so proud of his wife's beauty that he insisted his trusted bodyguard Gyges secretly see her undressed. Gyges begged him not to ask it, quoting an old proverb that a man should keep his eyes on what is his. The king insisted.

The queen noticed, and next day gave Gyges a terrible choice: kill the king or be killed. Gyges took the throne and founded a new dynasty.

Whatever the truth, the story's warning is clear: when we push others to cross lines for our vanity, the cost often falls back on us.
cards.quote: that each man should look on his own
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶9
cards.apply_it: Is there something you are pressing someone to do mainly to feed your own pride? Consider letting it go.

quiz.question: Why did Gyges at first refuse King Candaules' request?
options: He said each man should look on his own and the request was wrong
He was about to leave Lydia
He wanted to be paid first
quiz.explanation: Gyges answered with an old saying that each man should look on his own, and begged the king not to ask it.

cards.title: Before you attack, imagine what your rival is hoping you'll do
cards.body:
Croesus became king of Lydia, in western Turkey, around 560 BC and conquered the Greek cities of the coast. Next he planned to build a fleet to attack the Greek islands. Herodotus says a Greek sage, Bias of Priene (or Pittacus, by another account), stopped him with a joke.

The islanders were buying horses to attack Sardis, said Bias. Croesus laughed: he would love to meet sailors on horseback, where Lydia's famous cavalry ruled. Exactly, replied Bias, and the islanders would love to meet Lydians at sea. Croesus took the point and made friends with the islanders instead.

The lesson: fight on your strengths, not on ground your rival knows best.
cards.quote: what else however thinkest thou the men of the islands desire and have been praying for ever since the time they heard that thou wert about to build ships against them, than that they might catch the Lydians upon the sea
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶29
cards.apply_it: Before your next big move, write down what a competitor would most like you to do. Are you about to do it?

quiz.question: How did Bias persuade Croesus to drop his plan for a fleet?
options: He warned that ships were too costly
He told him the gods forbade it
He showed Croesus would be fighting on the islanders' home ground, the sea
He offered to build the ships himself
quiz.explanation: By joking about islanders on horseback, Bias showed that Lydians at sea would be as out of place as sailors in the saddle.

cards.title: The happiest man Solon knew was an ordinary citizen, not a rich king
cards.body:
Herodotus tells how Solon, the lawgiver of Athens, visited Croesus at Sardis. (Modern historians doubt the meeting, since their dates barely overlap, but the story became famous.) Croesus showed off his treasuries and then asked Solon who was the happiest man he had ever seen, expecting to hear his own name.

Solon named Tellos, an Athenian who lived while his city prospered, raised good children, saw grandchildren grow up, had enough to live on, and died honourably defending his home.

It is a quiet list: family, enough money, a community, a life that ends well. None of it can be shown off in a treasury, and all of it is within reach of ordinary people.
cards.quote: Tellos, in the first place, living while his native State was prosperous, had sons fair and good and saw from all of them children begotten and living to grow up
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶32
cards.apply_it: Write down three things on Tellos's list that you already have. Which one could you give more care this week?

quiz.question: Who did Solon name as the happiest man he had seen?
quiz.explanation: He chose Tellos, who had good children, enough to live on, a thriving city and an honourable death.

cards.title: Count no one happy until you see how their story ends
cards.body:
Croesus was annoyed that Solon did not rank him happiest. Solon explained that a seventy-year life holds over 26,000 days, and no day is exactly like another. A man may be rich and powerful now and ruined later. So he would call Croesus fortunate, but not yet happy, until he saw how his life ended.

Croesus thought him a fool for ignoring present riches. Within a few years, Herodotus tells us, Croesus had lost his son and his kingdom.

Solon was not being gloomy. He was asking us to hold good fortune lightly, to stay humble when things go well, and to judge a life by the whole of it, not by its best season.
cards.quote: but before he comes to his end it is well to hold back and not to call him yet happy but only fortunate
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶34
cards.apply_it: Think of something going well for you right now. Say 'I am fortunate' instead of 'I've made it', and notice how it feels.

quiz.question: What did Solon say he would call Croesus while he was still alive?
quiz.explanation: Solon would only call him fortunate, holding back the word happy until he saw how Croesus's life ended.

cards.title: A grieving king forgave the man who had killed his son by accident
cards.body:
Herodotus tells that Croesus dreamed his son Atys would be killed by an iron spear. Terrified, he kept Atys from war and even moved the weapons out of the men's rooms. But when a wild boar ravaged nearby farms, Atys begged to join the hunt. Croesus sent along a guest, Adrastos, to protect him. Adrastos threw a spear at the boar, missed, and killed Atys.

Adrastos came before the king and asked to be put to death. Croesus, in the depths of his own grief, pitied him instead, saying he had acted against his own will.

The story teaches two things: we cannot wrap the people we love in safety forever, and an accident is not a crime.
cards.quote: not thou alone art the cause of this evil, except in so far as thou wert the instrument of it against thine own will
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶46
cards.apply_it: Is there someone whose honest mistake you are still holding against them? Consider what forgiving them would free up in you.

quiz.question: How did Croesus respond when Adrastos asked to be killed?
options: He made him fight in the next war
He pitied him, saying he had acted against his will
quiz.explanation: Croesus saw that Adrastos was the unwilling instrument of the disaster, not its true cause, and pitied him.

cards.title: Croesus tested his advisers before trusting them with a big decision
cards.body:
Around 550 BC the Persians under Cyrus were growing fast, and Croesus wondered whether to strike first. He wanted divine advice, but which of the many Greek oracles could he trust?

Herodotus says he ran a test. Messengers went to seven oracles and, on the hundredth day after leaving Sardis, asked each what Croesus was doing at that moment. He had chosen something no one could guess: boiling a tortoise and a lamb together in a bronze pot. Only Delphi's answer, Herodotus says, described it.

Whatever we make of the oracles, the method is sound. Before trusting an adviser, a tool or a source with something important, check it against a question you already know the answer to.
cards.quote: he was sending the messengers abroad to the end that he might try the Oracles and find out what knowledge they had
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶48
cards.apply_it: Before relying on a new source of advice, test it with a question you already know the answer to.

quiz.question: What was the point of Croesus's tortoise-and-lamb test?
options: To honour the gods of Lydia
To check which oracles really had knowledge before asking his real question
quiz.explanation: He wanted to find out which oracle could be trusted before asking whether to attack Persia.

cards.title: "You will destroy a great empire" did not say whose
cards.body:
Having picked Delphi as the true oracle, Croesus asked whether to march on Persia. The answer: if he did, he would destroy a great empire. Delighted, he crossed the river Halys around 547 BC. After an indecisive battle and a siege, Cyrus took Sardis and Croesus was captured. The great empire destroyed was his own.

Later Croesus sent his chains to Delphi in protest. According to Herodotus, the priestess replied that he should have asked which empire was meant. He had heard what he wanted to hear.

When an answer seems to promise exactly what you hoped, that is the moment to ask one more question.
cards.quote: if he wished to take counsel well, ought to have sent and asked further whether the god meant his own empire or that of Cyrus
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶103
cards.apply_it: Think of advice you recently took as good news. What follow-up question would test whether you heard it right?

quiz.question: According to Delphi's reply, what was Croesus's real mistake?
options: Not asking which empire the oracle meant
quiz.explanation: The oracle said he should have asked whether it meant his own empire or Cyrus's.

cards.title: Deiokes became king by being the fairest judge in a lawless land
cards.body:
Herodotus tells how the Medes, in what is now north-western Iran, lived in scattered villages full of lawlessness. A man named Deiokes set out to be scrupulously fair in settling disputes. Word spread, and people from other villages brought him their cases until they trusted no one else.

Then Deiokes announced he was too busy with his own affairs to judge any more. Disorder returned, and the Medes decided they needed a king. They chose him. Herodotus notes he was ambitious all along, and once in power he built a walled capital, Ecbatana, and kept himself hidden from his old equals.

Fairness built his reputation; reputation built his power. Trust earned in small matters is how people come to lead in large ones.
cards.quote: And the Medes of the same village, seeing his manners, chose him for their judge.
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶110
cards.apply_it: Where could you be noticeably fair this week, in a small dispute or decision that others will see?

quiz.question: How did Deiokes first win the trust of the Medes?
options: By claiming to be sent by the gods
quiz.explanation: His reputation as a fair judge spread from village to village until the Medes made him king.

cards.title: Herodotus's legend of Cyrus: the herdsman's son the other boys chose as king
cards.body:
Herodotus tells a legend of Cyrus the Great's childhood. His grandfather Astyages, king of the Medes, dreamed the baby would one day replace him and ordered him killed. The order passed down until a royal herdsman and his wife, whose own baby had just died, raised Cyrus as theirs.

At ten, playing in the village, the other boys chose him as their 'king'. He handed out jobs, from builders to messengers, and punished a nobleman's son who disobeyed. The complaint brought him before Astyages, who recognised him.

Historians treat this as legend, but it captures something real: people tend to follow someone who gives everyone a clear part to play.
cards.quote: And the boys in their play chose as their king this one who was called the son of the herdsman
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶128
cards.apply_it: In your next group task, try giving each person one clear job. Notice how it changes the way the group works.

quiz.question: In Herodotus's legend, what did the boy Cyrus do as 'king' of the village children?
options: He gave each boy a job to do
He ran away to the city
quiz.explanation: He appointed builders, guards and messengers, giving each boy a role.

cards.title: Herodotus showed how a homely detail grew into a miracle story
cards.body:
A popular tale said baby Cyrus had been nursed by a dog. Herodotus offers a down-to-earth explanation. The herdsman's wife who raised Cyrus was named Kyno, which sounds like the Greek word for dog. When Cyrus returned to his real parents he praised her constantly. They then spread the story that a dog had nursed him, so that Persians would think his survival was supernatural.

Whether or not this explanation is right, it shows a historian at work: when a story sounds miraculous, look for the ordinary fact underneath and ask who gained from the telling.

Modern leaders' origin stories deserve the same gentle scepticism.
cards.quote: in order that their son might be thought by the Persians to have been preserved in a more supernatural manner
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶136
cards.apply_it: Pick a heroic origin story you've heard about a famous person or company. What ordinary fact might sit underneath it?

quiz.question: According to Herodotus, how did the story of Cyrus being nursed by a dog begin?
options: A dog really did nurse him
His nurse was named Kyno, and his parents turned this into a miracle tale
Cyrus made it up as a child
quiz.explanation: Herodotus says his parents built on the nurse's name, Kyno, to make his survival seem more wondrous.

cards.title: Cyrus let the Persians feel the difference between two futures
cards.body:
Around 550 BC the Persians, in what is now south-west Iran, were subjects of the Medes. Herodotus tells how Cyrus won them over to revolt. One day he had them clear a huge thorny field with sickles, a long, hard day. The next day he invited them, washed and rested, to a great feast in a meadow.

Then he asked which day they preferred. Obviously the second. Follow me, he said, and every day can be like this; stay as you are, and you will have endless days like yesterday.

Cyrus did not just argue for change. He let people feel both futures for themselves. A concrete experience often persuades where words alone fail.
cards.quote: If ye will do as I say, ye have these and ten thousand other good things, with no servile labour
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶140
cards.apply_it: When you want to persuade someone, can you let them experience the difference, through a demo, a trial or a visit, instead of only describing it?

quiz.question: How did Cyrus persuade the Persians to revolt against the Medes?
options: He paid each man in gold
He gave them a day of hard labour followed by a feast, then asked which they preferred
quiz.explanation: By contrasting a day of toil with a day of feasting, he made the choice feel obvious.

cards.title: A cruel king's own trusted servant helped bring him down
cards.body:
Astyages had ordered his most trusted noble, Harpagos, to kill the infant Cyrus. When he found the child still alive, Herodotus says, he punished Harpagos with a horrifying act of revenge against his own son. Harpagos waited for years, then secretly encouraged Cyrus to rebel and, when the Median army met the Persians, many deserted.

Around 550 BC Astyages lost his kingdom. Herodotus puts it bluntly: the Medes fell under Persian rule because of his cruelty. Cyrus, for his part, did Astyages no further harm and kept him at his court until he died.

Fear can make people obey for a while. It also creates enemies who are patient.
cards.quote: the Medes stooped under the yoke of the Persians because of his cruelty
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶144
cards.apply_it: Think of a time someone treated you harshly. How did it change your loyalty to them? Let that guide how you treat people under you.

quiz.question: According to Herodotus, why did the Medes end up under Persian rule?
options: Because the Medes chose Cyrus in an election
quiz.explanation: He says plainly that it happened because of the cruelty of their king, Astyages.

cards.title: On the pyre, Croesus remembered Solon and Cyrus remembered he was mortal
cards.body:
When Sardis fell, around 547 BC, Herodotus says Croesus was placed bound on a great pyre. As the flames were lit he cried out Solon's name three times. Cyrus asked why. Croesus told him how Solon had warned that no one should be called happy while still alive.

Cyrus, Herodotus says, reflected that he too was only human and that nothing people possess is secure. He ordered the fire put out. In the legend, a sudden rainstorm finished the job.

Historians doubt the details, and other sources hint Croesus may have died at Sardis. But the moment the story captures is real: a victor seeing himself in the defeated man, and choosing mercy.
cards.quote: considered that he himself also was but a man
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶98
cards.apply_it: When someone you have beaten in an argument or a contest is at a low point, picture yourself in their place before you act.

quiz.question: What made Cyrus change his mind about burning Croesus, according to Herodotus?
options: He reflected that he too was only a man and nothing was secure
quiz.explanation: Hearing Solon's warning, Cyrus saw that his own fortune could change too.

cards.title: In peace sons bury their fathers; in war fathers bury their sons
cards.body:
Rescued from the pyre, Croesus was asked by Cyrus why he had ever marched against him. Croesus blamed the oracle that had encouraged him, and then said one of the most quoted lines in Herodotus.

Nobody, he said, is so senseless as to choose war over peace. In peace, the natural order holds: children outlive their parents and bury them. In war that order is reversed, and parents bury their children.

The line has been repeated for 2,500 years because it puts the cost of war in the plainest human terms. Before any conflict, at home or between nations, it is worth asking who will carry its cost.
cards.quote: For no one is so senseless as to choose of his own will war rather peace, since in peace the sons bury their fathers, but in war the fathers bury their sons.
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶99
cards.apply_it: In a conflict you are part of, ask: who will pay the price if this escalates? Let that answer shape your next step.

quiz.question: According to Croesus, what happens to families in war?
quiz.explanation: War reverses the natural order, so that parents end up burying their children.

cards.title: "It is your wealth they are carrying away"
cards.body:
As Persian soldiers plundered Sardis, the captive Croesus asked Cyrus what they were doing. Plundering your city, said Cyrus. No, replied Croesus: it is no longer mine. It is your wealth they are taking.

He then warned that whichever soldier grabbed the most loot might become a rival. Herodotus says he suggested that guards at the gates take a tenth of the goods as an offering to the gods, so the men would give them up without resentment. Cyrus was delighted and followed the advice.

Two lessons sit here. A defeated rival can become a valuable adviser. And once something becomes yours, its protection becomes your responsibility.
cards.quote: Neither is it my city that they are plundering nor my wealth which they are carrying away; for I have no longer any property in these things: but it is thy wealth that they are carrying and driving away.
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶100
cards.apply_it: Is there someone you once competed with whose experience could help you now? Consider asking their advice.

quiz.question: What point did Croesus make to Cyrus about the plunder of Sardis?
options: The wealth now belonged to Cyrus, so his own men were taking from him
The gods would punish the Persians
quiz.explanation: Croesus pointed out that Sardis now belonged to Cyrus, so the looting was costing Cyrus himself.

cards.title: Persian boys were taught three things: ride, shoot and tell the truth
cards.body:
Describing Persian customs of the 400s BC, Herodotus says boys were educated from age five to twenty in only three things: riding, archery and speaking the truth. He adds that Persians thought lying the most disgraceful thing of all, and owing money the next worst, partly because debtors are pushed into lying.

He also admired a Persian rule that no one, not even the king, should put a person to death for a single offence, but should weigh their wrongs against their good service.

The idea that honesty belongs in a curriculum beside practical skills is worth keeping. Children learn truthfulness the way they learn to ride: by practice, and by watching adults do it.
cards.quote: And they educate their children, beginning at five years old and going on till twenty, in three things only, in riding, in shooting, and in speaking the truth
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶150
cards.apply_it: Name the three things you most want the young people around you to learn. Is honesty on the list, and do they see you practise it?

quiz.question: Which was one of the three things Herodotus says Persian boys were taught?
quiz.explanation: Riding, shooting and speaking the truth made up the whole of their education.

cards.title: The Persians checked every big decision in two different states of mind
cards.body:
Herodotus reports an unusual Persian custom. They discussed their most important affairs at feasts, after plenty of wine. The next day, when everyone was sober, the host put the decision to them again. If they still liked it, they adopted it; if not, they dropped it. And a decision first made sober was reconsidered over wine.

No one needs the wine. But the principle is sound: a choice that only looks good in one mood, whether excited, tired, angry or cautious, may not be a good choice. Testing it from a second state of mind catches errors that the first mood hides.
cards.quote: and if it pleases them when they are sober also, they adopt it, but if it does not please them, they let it go
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶147
cards.apply_it: For your next big decision, sleep on it and look at it again in a different mood before you commit.

quiz.question: What did the Persians do with a decision made at a feast, according to Herodotus?
options: Reconsidered it the next day when sober
Asked a priest to approve it
quiz.explanation: They put it to the test again when sober, and adopted it only if it still seemed good.

cards.title: Cyrus lost a whole summer punishing a river
cards.body:
In 539 BC, on his way to attack Babylon, Cyrus reached the river Gyndes, a tributary of the Tigris in what is now Iraq. One of his sacred white horses tried to swim across and was swept away. Herodotus says Cyrus was so furious with the river that he swore to make it so weak a person could wade it without wetting their knees.

He set his army to dig 360 channels to scatter its water. The work took the whole summer, and the campaign against Babylon waited until the next spring.

It is a vivid picture of anger costing more than the original loss. Before pouring energy into getting even, ask what the effort will cost you.
cards.quote: they spent the whole summer season at this spot working
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶207
cards.apply_it: Next time something frustrates you, ask: how much time will getting back at it cost me, and is it worth it?

quiz.question: Why did Cyrus spend a summer digging channels at the river Gyndes?
options: In anger, to punish the river for drowning his sacred horse
quiz.explanation: Furious that the river had swept away his horse, he divided it into 360 channels, delaying his campaign.

cards.title: Babylon thought its walls made it safe, and kept dancing as it fell
cards.body:
Babylon, near modern Baghdad, had stored food for years and felt secure behind its walls. In 539 BC, Herodotus says, Cyrus diverted the Euphrates into a marsh until the riverbed was shallow enough to wade, and his soldiers slipped into the city along it.

The city was so large, he adds, that people in the centre did not know the outskirts had fallen. They were holding a festival and went on dancing until the truth reached them. Babylonian records suggest the city actually opened its gates with little fighting, so the details may be legend.

The lesson holds either way: the defences you rely on most can make you stop watching.
cards.quote: they went on dancing and rejoicing during this time until they learnt the truth only too well
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶209
cards.apply_it: What is your 'city wall', the thing that makes you feel safe? Spend ten minutes checking whether it still protects you.

quiz.question: How, according to Herodotus, did the Persians get into Babylon?
options: By scaling the walls at night
By lowering the Euphrates and entering along the riverbed
Through a traitor who opened the gates
quiz.explanation: Cyrus diverted the river so his soldiers could wade in along the riverbed. Babylonian records tell a less dramatic story.

cards.title: Queen Tomyris told Cyrus to rule his own people and leave hers alone
cards.body:
After Babylon, Cyrus marched against the Massagetai, nomads east of the Caspian Sea in Central Asia, ruled by Queen Tomyris after her husband's death. He first tried to win her kingdom by proposing marriage. She saw through it.

As Cyrus built bridges to cross the Araxes river, she sent him a message: stop. You cannot know whether this will turn out well for you. Be content to rule your own people, and let us rule ours. She added that she knew he would not listen.

Her advice is one of history's clearest calls for restraint. Success can make any next conquest seem natural. Knowing when you have enough is a skill.
cards.quote: cease to do so, I say, and be king over thine own people, and endure to see us ruling those whom we rule.
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶225
cards.apply_it: Where in your life are you pushing for 'more' out of habit? Write down what 'enough' would look like there.

quiz.question: What did Tomyris advise Cyrus to do?
options: Rule his own people and leave hers alone
quiz.explanation: She urged him to stop, rule his own people, and let her people be.

cards.title: Fortune is a wheel that doesn't let the same people stay on top
cards.body:
By now Croesus had become an adviser at Cyrus's court. Debating how to fight Tomyris, he told Cyrus that his own bitter sufferings had become lessons in wisdom. If Cyrus thought he and his army were immortal, he said, advice was useless. But if he knew he was a mortal man leading mortal men, he should remember that human affairs turn like a wheel, and no one stays fortunate for ever.

It is a striking change from the proud king who once laughed at Solon. Loss had taught him what success never could.

Remembering the wheel keeps us humble at the top and hopeful at the bottom.
cards.quote: for the affairs of men there is a revolving wheel, and that this in its revolution suffers not the same persons always to have good fortune
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶226
cards.apply_it: If things are going well, name one way to stay humble. If they are going badly, remember the wheel is still turning.

quiz.question: What image did Croesus use to describe human fortune?
quiz.explanation: He said human affairs turn like a wheel that does not let the same people always prosper.

cards.title: Cyrus the Great died in a campaign he didn't need to fight
cards.body:
Herodotus says Cyrus was driven against the Massagetai partly because people believed he was more than mortal, and because no nation had ever escaped him. Following Croesus's advice, he left a feast of wine in his camp; the Massagetai who captured it got drunk and were overwhelmed. Tomyris's son was taken prisoner and took his own life.

The queen then gave battle, around 530 BC, and Herodotus calls it the fiercest fight between non-Greeks he knew of. Most of the Persian army died, and Cyrus with it. Herodotus admits there were many accounts of Cyrus's death and gives the one he found most believable; the Greek writer Xenophon later said he died peacefully at home.

An unbroken run of wins can be the most dangerous thing a leader has.
cards.quote: Now as regards the end of the life of Cyrus there are many tales told, but this which I have related is to my mind the most worthy of belief.
cards.locator: Book I. The First Book of the Histories, Called Clio ¶233
cards.apply_it: After a run of success, ask a trusted person: what risk am I taking only because things have gone well so far?

quiz.question: How did Herodotus handle the many stories about Cyrus's death?
options: He gave the one he found most believable and said others existed
quiz.explanation: He admitted there were many tales and chose the one that seemed to him most worthy of belief.

cards.title: Herodotus checked what the Egyptians told him against his own eyes
cards.body:
Egyptian priests told Herodotus that much of their land had once been sea, built up by the Nile's mud. He agreed, and his reasons are what make the passage remarkable. He noticed that Egypt juts further into the sea than its neighbours, that seashells lie on its hills, that salt crusts form on the ground, and that its soil is black silt quite unlike the red sand of Libya or the clay of Arabia. Even a day's sail offshore, a sounding line brought up mud.

His famous phrase was that Egypt is the gift of the river.

He heard a claim, then went looking for evidence that could confirm or disprove it. That is the heart of good thinking in any field.
cards.quote: I have observed that Egypt runs out into the sea further than the adjoining land, and that shells are found upon the mountains of it
cards.locator: Book II. The Second Book of the Histories, Called Euterpe ¶13
cards.apply_it: Take one thing you believe because someone told you. What could you observe for yourself that would confirm or challenge it?

quiz.question: What evidence did Herodotus use to support the idea that Egypt was built by the Nile?
options: Shells on the hills, black silt soil and mud far offshore
quiz.explanation: He pointed to physical signs: shells on hills, salt, silty black soil and mud brought up far out at sea.

cards.title: An Egyptian king tried an experiment, and Herodotus checked three cities' versions
cards.body:
Psammetichus I ruled Egypt from 664 to 610 BC. Herodotus says he wanted to know which people were the oldest, so he had two newborns raised by a shepherd who never spoke in their presence. After two years they said 'bekos', which turned out to be the Phrygian word for bread, so the Egyptians conceded the Phrygians were older.

The experiment was cruel to the children and its logic is faulty. But note what Herodotus did next: he travelled to Thebes and Heliopolis to see if their priests agreed with those at Memphis, and dismissed a lurid Greek version as an idle tale.

One source is a rumour. Several that agree begin to be evidence.
cards.quote: I wished to know whether the priests at these places would agree in their accounts with those at Memphis
cards.locator: Book II. The Second Book of the Histories, Called Euterpe ¶4
cards.apply_it: Next time a surprising claim reaches you, look for two independent sources before you repeat it.

quiz.question: Why did Herodotus visit Thebes and Heliopolis?
options: To check whether their priests' accounts agreed with those at Memphis
quiz.explanation: He wanted to compare independent accounts rather than rely on one group of informants.

cards.title: One counterexample can knock down a confident theory
cards.body:
Why does the Nile flood every summer when other rivers shrink? Greek thinkers had offered several explanations. One said the seasonal Etesian winds held back the river's flow into the sea.

Herodotus tested it with two facts. The winds often fail, yet the Nile floods anyway. And many other rivers in Syria and Libya also face those winds, but do not flood. So the theory could not be right. Another theory, about a river called Ocean surrounding the world, he dismissed as a poet's invention that could not be checked.

We now know the flood comes from summer rains in the Ethiopian highlands. But his method still works: if a cause is real, it should show up every time.
cards.quote: But often the Etesian Winds fail and yet the Nile does the same work as it is wont to do
cards.locator: Book II. The Second Book of the Histories, Called Euterpe ¶22
cards.apply_it: Take an explanation you've heard for something in your life. Can you think of a case where the 'cause' was present but the effect wasn't?

quiz.question: How did Herodotus refute the theory that winds caused the Nile flood?
options: He noted the Nile floods even when the winds fail, and other rivers facing the winds do not flood
quiz.explanation: He used counterexamples: the effect happened without the supposed cause, and the cause occurred without the effect.

cards.title: Egyptian priests answered a boast about divine ancestry with 345 ordinary men
cards.body:
Before Herodotus, the Greek writer Hecataeus visited the temple at Thebes in Egypt and proudly traced his family back sixteen generations to a god. The priests showed him the wooden statues of their high priests, one set up by each in his lifetime, 345 in all, each the son of the one before.

Not one of them, they said, descended from a god or hero. Each was simply a 'piromis', which Herodotus explains means an honourable and good man.

It is a gentle put-down of family pride. A long line of decent people is worth more than a famous name, and we are judged by how we live, not by whom we came from.
cards.quote: and neither with a god nor a hero did they connect their descent.
cards.locator: Book II. The Second Book of the Histories, Called Euterpe ¶155
cards.apply_it: Think of an ancestor or elder whose quiet goodness you admire. What one habit of theirs could you carry on?

quiz.question: What did the Egyptian priests call each of the 345 high priests in their line?
options: A 'piromis', an honourable and good man
quiz.explanation: They traced no god or hero, only generation after generation of honourable and good men.

cards.title: Egypt remembered its pyramid-builders with resentment and a just king with praise
cards.body:
Herodotus heard from Egyptian priests that Khufu (whom he calls Cheops), builder of the Great Pyramid around 2560 BC, closed the temples and forced the people to labour for him. Egyptians, he says, so disliked him and his successor that they would hardly speak their names. Archaeology today suggests the builders were organised, fed workers rather than slaves, so the priests' account is coloured.

The next king, Menkaure (Mykerinos), reopened the temples, freed people to return to their own work, and judged so fairly that if someone was unhappy with a verdict he compensated them from his own wealth.

Monuments can last for millennia, but a ruler's reputation is built in how ordinary people were treated.
cards.quote: for he not only gave good decisions, but also when a man complained of the decision, he gave him recompense from his own goods and thus satisfied his desire.
cards.locator: Book II. The Second Book of the Histories, Called Euterpe ¶140
cards.apply_it: When someone is unhappy with a decision you made, could you acknowledge their loss even if the decision stands?

quiz.question: Why did Egyptians praise King Mykerinos, according to Herodotus?
options: He judged fairly and compensated people unhappy with his verdicts
quiz.explanation: He reopened the temples, freed the people, and even repaid those who complained of his rulings.

cards.title: The Egyptians spotted a conflict of interest in the Olympic Games
cards.body:
Around 590 BC, under King Psammis (Psammetichus II), envoys came to Egypt from Elis, the Greek city that ran the Olympic Games. They boasted that their rules were perfectly fair and asked if the wise Egyptians could improve them.

The Egyptians asked one question: could citizens of Elis compete? Yes, anyone could. Then, said the Egyptians, the games were not fair, because the judges would inevitably favour their own people over strangers. If they truly wanted justice, the hosts should not compete.

It is a 2,600-year-old statement of a modern rule: people should not judge contests in which they or their own have a stake.
cards.quote: for it could not be but that they would take part with the man of their own State, if he was contending, and so act unfairly to the stranger
cards.locator: Book II. The Second Book of the Histories, Called Euterpe ¶176
cards.apply_it: Are you judging anything, a hire, a contest, a dispute, where someone close to you is involved? Consider stepping back or bringing in another judge.

quiz.question: What flaw did the Egyptians find in how Elis ran the Olympic Games?
options: Elis citizens could compete while Elis judges ran the games
quiz.explanation: Judges from Elis would naturally favour their own citizens, so the hosts should not compete.

cards.title: Amasis turned a gold foot-basin into a lesson about status
cards.body:
Amasis, who ruled Egypt from about 570 to 526 BC, was a commoner who came to power through a soldiers' revolt. At first Egyptians looked down on him for his humble birth. Herodotus says he won them over 'by wisdom and not wilfulness'.

He had a gold foot-basin, used for washing feet and worse, melted down and recast as a statue of a god, which people began to worship. Then he told them where the gold had come from. Like the basin, he said, he had once been ordinary; now he was their king, and deserved respect.

He made his point with a story people could see. Origins don't decide what someone becomes.
cards.quote: afterwards Amasis won them over to himself by wisdom and not wilfulness
cards.locator: Book II. The Second Book of the Histories, Called Euterpe ¶188
cards.apply_it: Is there someone whose background makes you underrate them? Look for one thing they do well this week.

quiz.question: How did Amasis convince Egyptians to respect him despite his humble birth?
options: By showing that a worshipped statue had been made from a humble foot-basin
quiz.explanation: The statue showed that what something becomes matters more than what it was made from.

cards.title: A bow kept always strung will break: Amasis on rest
cards.body:
Amasis worked hard every morning until the market filled, handling business willingly. After that he relaxed, drank and joked with his friends. His advisers complained that a king should sit solemnly on his throne all day.

He answered with an image. Archers string their bows when they need them and unstring them afterwards; a bow kept tight all the time will break just when you need it. People are the same: someone who is always serious and never relaxes will crack before they realise it.

Rest is not the opposite of good work. It is part of it. Building regular downtime into your day protects your ability to perform when it counts.
cards.quote: if he should always be in earnest and not relax himself for sport at the due time, he would either go mad or be struck with stupor before he was aware
cards.locator: Book II. The Second Book of the Histories, Called Euterpe ¶189
cards.apply_it: Block out one guilt-free stretch of rest in your calendar this week and protect it like a meeting.

quiz.question: What image did Amasis use to defend his daily time off?
options: A lamp running out of oil
A bow that breaks if always kept strung
A horse that refuses to run
quiz.explanation: Like a bow, a person who is never 'unstrung' will snap when needed most.

cards.title: Polycrates threw his treasured ring into the sea, and a fish brought it back
cards.body:
Polycrates, ruler of the Greek island of Samos in the 530s and 520s BC, succeeded at everything. Herodotus says his friend Amasis of Egypt grew uneasy and wrote that he would rather have a life of mixed fortune than unbroken success, which usually ended badly. He urged Polycrates to throw away what he valued most.

Polycrates threw his precious emerald signet ring into the sea. Days later a fisherman brought a fine fish to the palace, and inside it was the ring. Amasis broke off the friendship, sure a disaster was coming. Years later a Persian governor lured Polycrates to his death.

It is a legend, but a thoughtful one: setbacks are part of a normal life, not a sign that it has failed.
cards.quote: I desire, both for myself and for those about whom I have care, that in some of our affairs we should be prosperous and in others should fail
cards.locator: Book III. The Third Book of the Histories, Called Thaleia ¶40
cards.apply_it: Recall a recent setback. Can you see it as part of a normal, mixed life rather than proof that things are going wrong?

quiz.question: What did Amasis advise Polycrates to do about his constant good fortune?
options: Throw away the thing he valued most
quiz.explanation: He urged him to cast away his most treasured possession, but the ring came back inside a fish.

cards.title: Psammenitus did not weep for his own children, but wept for an old friend
cards.body:
In 525 BC Cambyses, son of Cyrus, conquered Egypt. To test the captured king Psammenitus, he paraded the king's daughter dressed as a slave and then his son being led to execution. The other Egyptians wailed; Psammenitus only bowed his head. But when an elderly friend passed by, now reduced to begging, he cried aloud.

Asked why, he said his own sorrows were too great for tears, but his friend's fall called for weeping. Herodotus says even Cambyses was moved and tried, too late, to spare the son.

The story is a reminder that deep grief may be silent. A person who seems calm may be carrying more than anyone around them.
cards.quote: O son of Cyrus, my own troubles were too great for me to lament them aloud, but the trouble of my companion was such as called for tears
cards.locator: Book III. The Third Book of the Histories, Called Thaleia ¶14
cards.apply_it: Is someone around you going through a loss quietly? Check in on them gently, without expecting them to show it.

quiz.question: Why did Psammenitus not weep for his own children, according to his answer?
options: His own sorrows were too great for tears
quiz.explanation: He said his own troubles were beyond lamenting aloud, while his friend's misfortune called for tears.

cards.title: Cambyses could have been wise in spite of his mistake, if he had turned back
cards.body:
After Egypt, Cambyses sent spies to the 'Long-lived Ethiopians' far to the south, in what is now Sudan. Their king sent back a bow and a rebuke: a just man would not covet another's land.

Enraged, Herodotus says, Cambyses marched at once without arranging supplies. Before a fifth of the journey, food ran out; the soldiers ate their pack animals, then grass, and finally were driven to desperate horrors before he turned back, having lost many men.

Herodotus's judgement is fair: the first mistake was rash, but turning back when supplies failed would still have made him wise. Changing course early is not weakness. Pushing on to save face is what turns an error into a disaster.
cards.quote: Now if Cambyses when he perceived this had changed his plan and led his army back, he would have been a wise man
cards.locator: Book III. The Third Book of the Histories, Called Thaleia ¶25
cards.apply_it: Is there a plan you are continuing mainly to avoid admitting it isn't working? What would turning back now save?

quiz.question: According to Herodotus, when could Cambyses still have been called wise?
options: If he had never gone to Egypt
If he had turned back once his supplies ran out
If he had brought more soldiers
If he had asked an oracle
quiz.explanation: Turning back at the first sign of failure would have made him wise despite his first mistake.

cards.title: "I acted quickly rather than wisely": Cambyses and his brother
cards.body:
Herodotus tells that Cambyses envied his brother Smerdis, the only Persian able to draw the Ethiopian king's bow a little way. Then he dreamed of Smerdis on the throne, and secretly had him killed.

In 522 BC news came that 'Smerdis' had seized power. It was an impostor, a Magian priest of the same name. Cambyses realised his brother had died for nothing. Rushing to mount his horse, he wounded himself with his own sword and, dying, confessed to the Persian nobles.

Modern historians debate whether the 'false Smerdis' was really an impostor; Darius's own inscriptions told this version. But Cambyses' confession names a timeless failure: letting fear drive an irreversible act.
cards.quote: Fearing then lest I should be deprived of my power by my brother, I acted quickly rather than wisely
cards.locator: Book III. The Third Book of the Histories, Called Thaleia ¶67
cards.apply_it: Before you act on fear this week, wait a day and ask: is this reversible if I'm wrong?

quiz.question: What did Cambyses admit about the killing of his brother?
options: It was ordered by the gods
He had acted quickly rather than wisely, out of fear
quiz.explanation: He confessed that fear of losing power made him act quickly rather than wisely.

cards.title: Custom is king: everyone thinks their own ways are best
cards.body:
Herodotus believed Cambyses was mad partly because he mocked the religion and customs of the Egyptians. Everyone, Herodotus says, would choose their own customs as best if offered all the world's options.

He illustrates it with a story about Darius. The king asked some Greeks what price would make them eat their dead fathers' bodies; they said no price could. He then asked people from India called the Callatians, whose custom was to do exactly that, what would make them burn their dead as Greeks did. They cried out in horror. Herodotus quotes the poet Pindar: custom is king of all.

Remembering this makes it easier to approach other cultures with curiosity instead of contempt.
cards.quote: thus all think that their own customs are by far the best
cards.locator: Book III. The Third Book of the Histories, Called Thaleia ¶38
cards.apply_it: Pick one custom from another culture that seems strange to you. Look up why people practise it.

quiz.question: What did Darius's experiment with the Greeks and the Callatians show?
options: Each people found the other's funeral customs horrifying
quiz.explanation: Each group was appalled by the other's practice, showing that people judge by their own customs.

cards.title: Phaidyme risked her life to prove the new king was an impostor
cards.body:
Otanes, a Persian noble, suspected the man ruling as 'Smerdis' was the Magian impostor. That Magian, Herodotus says, had once had his ears cut off as a punishment. Otanes's daughter Phaidyme was among the king's wives, and he asked her to check, while the king slept, whether he had ears.

She knew that if he woke and caught her, he would kill her. She did it anyway, found no ears, and sent word to her father. Her discovery set in motion the plot of seven nobles that ended the impostor's rule in 522 BC.

History often remembers the men who struck the blow. The truth they acted on was uncovered at real personal risk by a young woman.
cards.quote: she would run a great risk; for supposing that he should chance not to have his ears, and she were detected feeling for them, she was well assured that he would put her to death; but nevertheless she would do this
cards.locator: Book III. The Third Book of the Histories, Called Thaleia ¶71
cards.apply_it: Who in your workplace or family quietly took a risk that made others' success possible? Thank them by name.

quiz.question: What did Phaidyme do to help expose the false king?
options: She checked whether he had ears while he slept
quiz.explanation: At great risk, she felt for his ears while he slept, confirming he was the Magian impostor.

cards.title: The first recorded debate on democracy, oligarchy and monarchy
cards.body:
After overthrowing the impostor in 522 BC, Herodotus says, the seven Persian conspirators debated how Persia should be ruled. He insists the speeches happened, though Greeks doubted it, and many historians still do.

Otanes argued for rule by the people: a monarch answers to no one, and even the best man is corrupted by unchecked power. Megabyzos argued for rule by a few of the best. Darius argued for one excellent ruler. Darius won, and Otanes withdrew, asking only that neither he nor his descendants be ruled by the others.

Otanes's central point still underpins modern government: power that never has to give an account of itself goes wrong.
cards.quote: how should the rule of one alone be a well-ordered thing, seeing that the monarch may do what he desires without rendering any account of his acts?
cards.locator: Book III. The Third Book of the Histories, Called Thaleia ¶82
cards.apply_it: Who holds you to account for the power you have, at work or at home? If no one does, invite someone to.

quiz.question: What was Otanes's main argument against rule by one man?
options: A monarch can do what he likes without answering for it, which corrupts even the best
quiz.explanation: He argued that unaccountable power corrupts even the best of men.

cards.title: Darius won the throne thanks to his groom, and said so in stone
cards.body:
The six remaining conspirators agreed that whoever's horse neighed first at sunrise would be king. Herodotus says Darius's clever groom, Oibares, arranged it with a trick involving a mare the horse favoured; Herodotus even gives two Persian versions of how it was done. Darius's horse neighed, thunder rolled, and the others bowed to him. He became king in 522 BC and ruled until 486 BC.

Darius then set up a carved relief, Herodotus says, crediting his kingdom to the excellence of his horse and his groom.

Whatever the truth of the tale, its point is worth keeping: people rarely rise alone, and naming those who helped you is both honest and wise.
cards.quote: Some say that the contrivance of Oibares was this, but others say as follows (for the story is told by the Persians in both ways)
cards.locator: Book III. The Third Book of the Histories, Called Thaleia ¶89
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent success. Who helped make it happen? Tell them, or tell others, what they did.

quiz.question: Whom did Darius's monument credit for his becoming king, according to Herodotus?
options: His horse and his groom Oibares
quiz.explanation: The carving credited his horse and his horse-keeper Oibares.

cards.title: Persians remembered Cyrus as a father, Cambyses as a master and Darius as a shopkeeper
cards.body:
Darius reorganised the empire into twenty provinces, called satrapies, each paying a fixed annual tribute. Under Cyrus and Cambyses, Herodotus says, people had simply brought gifts.

The Persians summed up their three kings in a saying. Darius was a shopkeeper, because he ran everything with careful accounts. Cambyses was a master, because he was harsh and cared little for anyone. Cyrus was a father, because he was gentle and arranged good things for all.

Each style says something about how leaders are remembered. Efficient systems earn respect; harshness earns fear; care earns love. The best leaders try to combine the shopkeeper's order with the father's warmth.
cards.quote: the Persians say that Dareios was a shopkeeper, Cambyses a master, and Cyrus a father
cards.locator: Book III. The Third Book of the Histories, Called Thaleia ¶91
cards.apply_it: How would the people you lead describe you in one word: shopkeeper, master or father? What one change would move you closer to the word you want?

quiz.question: Why did the Persians call Cyrus a 'father'?
options: He was gentle and provided good things for all
quiz.explanation: Cyrus was remembered as gentle and caring, Darius as businesslike, Cambyses as harsh.

cards.title: A cloak given freely to a nobody was repaid by a king
cards.body:
Years before he became king, Darius was a junior guardsman in Cambyses' army in Egypt. In the market at Memphis he admired a red cloak worn by Syloson, an exile from Samos, and offered to buy it. Syloson, on impulse, simply gave it to him.

When Syloson later heard that the same man was now king of Persia, he went to the palace and introduced himself as the king's benefactor. Darius remembered and said a gift given when he had no power counted as much as a great one now. Syloson asked not for gold but for his home island, and Darius restored him to Samos, though the takeover cost Samos dearly.

Kindness to people who can do nothing for you is never wasted.
cards.quote: thou art he who when as yet I had no power gavest me a gift, small it may be, but nevertheless the kindness is counted with me to be as great as if I should now receive some great thing from some one
cards.locator: Book III. The Third Book of the Histories, Called Thaleia ¶142
cards.apply_it: Do one small kindness this week for someone who can do nothing for you in return.

quiz.question: Why did Darius value Syloson's cloak so highly?
options: It brought him luck in battle
It was given freely when Darius had no power
quiz.explanation: A gift given before he was anyone counted, he said, as much as a great gift now.

cards.title: Darius said he would rather have his friend whole than twenty Babylons
cards.body:
When Babylon revolted against Darius, the Persian siege dragged on for many months. Herodotus says a noble named Zopyros devised a desperate plan: he disfigured himself, pretended Darius had done it, and defected to the Babylonians. Trusted by them, he rose to command and then opened the gates to the Persians.

Darius rewarded him richly, making him governor of Babylon for life. But Herodotus adds that Darius often said he would rather Zopyros had never been harmed than gain twenty more Babylons.

The story is about loyalty, but Darius's remark is the lasting lesson: no goal is worth more than the people who pay for it.
cards.quote: he would rather that Zopyros were free from the injury than that he should have twenty Babylons added to his possession
cards.locator: Book III. The Third Book of the Histories, Called Thaleia ¶162
cards.apply_it: Is a goal of yours costing someone close to you more than it should? Ask them how they are doing.

quiz.question: What did Darius often say about Zopyros's sacrifice?
options: It was a small price for Babylon
He would rather Zopyros were unharmed than gain twenty Babylons
It was a trick of the gods
quiz.explanation: He valued his friend's wellbeing above even twenty cities like Babylon.

cards.title: The Scythians couldn't be conquered because they had no city to lose
cards.body:
Around 513 BC Darius crossed into Europe to attack the Scythians, nomads of the steppes north of the Black Sea, in what is now Ukraine and southern Russia. Herodotus says they had found the one thing that made them unbeatable: they lived in wagons, lived by herds instead of farms, and fought as mounted archers. No one could pin them down.

They simply retreated, filling wells and stripping the land. When Darius demanded they fight or surrender, their king Idanthyrsos replied that they had no cities or crops to defend, so had no reason to fight until they chose.

An opponent with nothing fixed to attack is very hard to defeat. Flexibility can be a strength in itself.
cards.quote: We have neither cities nor land sown with crops, about which we should fear lest they should be captured or laid waste
cards.locator: Book IV. The Fourth Book of the Histories, Called Melpomene ¶130
cards.apply_it: Where are you most exposed because you're tied to one fixed thing, one client, one skill, one income? Take a step to loosen that.

quiz.question: Why could Darius not force the Scythians into battle?
options: They had no cities or farms to defend and kept moving
quiz.explanation: As nomads with no fixed cities or crops, they could retreat and choose when to fight.

cards.title: Darius read the Scythians' strange gifts as the answer he wanted
cards.body:
With his army struggling, Darius received gifts from the Scythians: a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows. The messenger refused to explain them.

Darius decided they meant surrender: earth (the mouse), water (the frog), horses (the bird, which is swift) and their weapons. His adviser Gobryas, one of the seven who had killed the impostor, read them differently: unless you Persians fly like birds, hide like mice or leap into lakes like frogs, these arrows will kill you before you get home.

Gobryas was right, and Darius soon retreated. When a message is unclear, the reading that flatters us most deserves the most doubt.
cards.quote: Unless ye become birds and fly up into the heaven, O Persians, or become mice and sink down under the earth, or become frogs and leap into the lakes, ye shall not return back home, but shall be smitten by these arrows.
cards.locator: Book IV. The Fourth Book of the Histories, Called Melpomene ¶135
cards.apply_it: Next time a message is ambiguous, write down the most flattering and least flattering readings, and ask someone else which fits better.

quiz.question: How did Darius first interpret the Scythian gifts?
quiz.explanation: He read them as surrender, but Gobryas saw them as a warning, and Gobryas was right.

cards.title: A junior commander told Darius to keep the bridge home, and was rewarded
cards.body:
When Darius's army crossed the Danube into Scythian land, he ordered the Greek sailors to dismantle the bridge of boats behind him. Coës, commander of the men from Mytilene on Lesbos, asked permission to speak. Keep the bridge, he said. We are entering land without towns or farms. If we win, we have a way home; if we can't even find the enemy, our retreat is still safe. And, he added, he would march on himself, so no one could say he wanted to stay behind.

Darius took the advice and promised to reward him. That bridge later saved the Persian army.

A good plan includes a way back. And good leaders listen to sound advice from below.
cards.quote: if we find the Scythians and fare as we desire, we have a way of return; and also even if we shall not be able to find them, at least our way of return is secured
cards.locator: Book IV. The Fourth Book of the Histories, Called Melpomene ¶100
cards.apply_it: For your current project, write down your 'bridge home': what you'll do if it doesn't go as planned.

quiz.question: What did Coës advise Darius to do with the bridge over the Danube?
options: Keep it guarded as a way home
quiz.explanation: He urged Darius to leave it standing so the army would have a secure route back.

cards.title: The Greek tyrants saved Darius because their own power depended on him
cards.body:
While Darius was in Scythia, Ionian Greeks guarded his Danube bridge. The Scythians urged them to destroy it, trap the Persians and win their freedom. Miltiades of Athens, ruler of the Chersonese (now the Gallipoli peninsula), agreed.

But Histiaios, tyrant of Miletus, pointed out that each of them ruled his city only because Darius backed him. If Persia fell, their cities would choose to be governed by the people instead. The others swung behind Histiaios, and the bridge was kept.

It shows how private interest can quietly decide public questions. When someone argues for a course of action, it is fair to ask what they personally stand to gain.
cards.quote: for each of the cities would choose to have popular rather than despotic rule
cards.locator: Book IV. The Fourth Book of the Histories, Called Melpomene ¶140
cards.apply_it: When you hear a strong argument this week, ask: what does the person making it stand to gain or lose?

quiz.question: Why did Histiaios argue against destroying Darius's bridge?
options: His own power as tyrant depended on Persian support
quiz.explanation: He knew that without Darius the cities would choose popular rule over tyrants like him.

cards.title: The detail Herodotus doubted is what makes the story believable
cards.body:
Herodotus reports that Necho II, king of Egypt from about 610 to 595 BC, sent Phoenician sailors south down the Red Sea to sail around Africa (which the Greeks called Libya). Each autumn they landed, sowed grain and waited for the harvest. In the third year they came back through the Strait of Gibraltar.

They reported that as they sailed west around the south of Africa, the sun was on their right, to the north. Herodotus could not believe it. Yet that is exactly what happens south of the equator, which is why many historians think the voyage really happened.

An odd detail that a storyteller had no reason to invent can be the strongest evidence of all.
cards.quote: And they reported a thing which I cannot believe, but another man may, namely that in sailing round Libya they had the sun on their right hand.
cards.locator: Book IV. The Fourth Book of the Histories, Called Melpomene ¶44
cards.apply_it: When you hear a strange detail in a story, ask whether anyone would have reason to make it up.

quiz.question: Why do historians take the reported sun 'on the right hand' as evidence the voyage happened?
options: It is what sailors would really see south of the equator
It was confirmed by an oracle
quiz.explanation: South of the equator the noon sun is to the north, exactly what the sailors reported and Herodotus doubted.

cards.title: Report what people say, and say plainly when you don't believe it
cards.body:
Herodotus was often called the 'father of lies' for including tall tales. But he usually signposted them. Writing about the Neuri, a people north of the Scythians, he passes on the claim that each of them turns into a wolf for a few days a year, then adds that he does not believe it, though people swear to it.

He does the same with men said to have goats' feet or to sleep six months a year. Elsewhere he states his rule outright: he writes down what people in each place told him, and readers may believe it if they find it credible.

It is still a sound way to share information: separate what you were told from what you know.
cards.quote: For my part I do not believe them when they say this, but they say it nevertheless, and swear it moreover.
cards.locator: Book IV. The Fourth Book of the Histories, Called Melpomene ¶108
cards.apply_it: Next time you pass on something you heard, add one honest phrase: 'I've checked this' or 'I haven't checked this'.

quiz.question: How did Herodotus handle the story that the Neuri turned into wolves?
options: He reported it but said he did not believe it
He said he had seen it
quiz.explanation: He recorded what people claimed, and clearly stated his own disbelief.
